world_behind.title: A sermon with its reading behind it
world_behind.text: Jacob opens by saying why he read two chapters of Isaiah aloud: "I have read these things that ye might know concerning the covenants of the Lord" (v. 1). 2 Nephi 7 and 8 carry Isaiah 50 and 51, which is the reading he means. Everything that follows is exposition. The colony has just heard the servant beaten and the city told to stand up, and now their preacher explains what makes either possible.

cites.quote: I have read these things that ye might know concerning the covenants of the Lord

spans.text: I have read these things that ye might know concerning the covenants of the Lord

world_behind.title: The oldest full account of the plan in the record
world_behind.text: Lehi gave his version to Jacob privately (2 Ne. 2); this is the first time the whole sequence, fall, death, resurrection, judgment, is preached to a congregation. What later writers assume, this chapter argues. That is why Alma, Amulek, and Mormon can be brief where Jacob is thorough.

world_behind.title: A people who had watched a father die
world_behind.text: 2 Nephi 4:12 records Lehi's death, two chapters and a few years back. Nothing focuses a colony on resurrection like a fresh grave, and the sermon's opening move is to grant the fact before answering it: "our flesh must waste away and die; nevertheless, in our bodies we shall see God" (v. 4).

cites.quote: our flesh must waste away and die; nevertheless, in our bodies we shall see God

spans.text: our flesh must waste away and die; nevertheless, in our bodies we shall see God

world_behind.title: Names for the enemy
world_behind.text: The chapter calls the adversary the devil, the father of lies, the angel who fell, the cunning one, and the devil of all devils. Israelite writers before the exile rarely spoke of him at such length. Jacob's picture is unusually full, and its source is stated: he is teaching what the angel and the prophets gave him, not speculating.

world_behind.title: The wo-list as a form
world_behind.text: Verses 27 through 38 stack ten pronouncements in a row, each naming a class and its end. Isaiah 5:8 to 22 uses the form on a nation; Jacob turns it on a congregation of perhaps a few hundred people, including the learned, the rich, and the deaf, which in a settlement that size means specific faces.

world_behind.title: A sermon delivered over two days
world_behind.text: The chapter ends with a scheduling note: "on the morrow I will declare unto you the remainder of my words" (v. 54). 2 Nephi 10:1 opens with the remainder, and 2 Nephi 10:3 reports an angel visiting him between the two sessions. What the colony heard in one sitting was the reading plus this exposition, and they went home overnight with the wos and the invitation both still ringing. Jacob says at the start of the next day's preaching that an angel spoke to him during that night, so the pause was not only for the hearers' benefit.

cites.quote: on the morrow I will declare unto you the remainder of my words

spans.text: on the morrow I will declare unto you the remainder of my words

words.text: Jacob's word for what a situation requires, and he uses it three times at three different levels. Treated at 1 Nephi 10:15. It is expedient that the Messiah show himself at Jerusalem (v. 5); expedient that Jacob wake his hearers to "an awful reality" (v. 47); expedient that he teach the consequences of sin because they are not holy (v. 48). The term names necessity that comes from circumstances, and by the third use he is applying it to his own harshness.

A small adverb doing the chapter's hardest work. "They who are righteous shall be righteous still, and they who are filthy shall be filthy still" (v. 16). The word means continuing, unchanged by the event that has just occurred. Judgment in this verse does not create the two classes; it finds them, which is why the sermon spends its second half on what a person is becoming now.

cites.quote: They who are righteous shall be righteous still, and they who are filthy shall be filthy still

spans.text: They who are righteous shall be righteous still, and they who are filthy shall be filthy still

words.text: The term arrived in the record at 1 Nephi 10:21 as a name for mortal life under test. Jacob adds the one thing the earlier use lacks: it can be wasted. "That wasteth the days of his probation" (v. 27) puts the trial's value in its limited supply, and the wo attaches to spending the time on nothing.

cites.quote: That wasteth the days of his probation

spans.text: That wasteth the days of his probation

words.text: A farming word, and a violent one: the harrow is dragged over broken ground to tear it up before planting. Jacob asks whether he would harrow up souls whose minds were pure, and the answer is no. The image concedes that his preaching hurts and insists the hurt is preparation. Later writers in the record use the word for what guilt does to a person without any preacher's help.

Richness, the good part of the meal, an idea of plenty that a subsistence colony would feel in the stomach. It comes to Jacob out of Isaiah 55 and sits at the end of a chapter that has spent its length on fire, chains, and a monster. The sermon's last picture of salvation is not escape. It is dinner.

Nephi met the word in the singular when an angel asked him whether he knew "the condescension of God" (1 Ne. 11:16). Jacob makes it plural and puts it in a list with covenants, grace, and mercy. What the brother saw once in vision, the brother-preacher counts as a habit, and what the plural buys is a God who has come down more than once and will again.

phrases.text: Said twice in one sentence, once as a requirement and once as the condition of everything after it. The argument is arithmetic: a death that lasts endlessly can only be undone by something without limits, so a finite offering leaves the flesh to "crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more" (v. 7). Only one other preacher in the record uses the phrase, and Amulek uses it to answer a lawyer's question about the law's demands. Jacob is answering the fall itself.

cites.quote: crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more

spans.text: crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more

phrases.term: O the wisdom of God, his mercy and grace!
phrases.text: Seven exclamations open verses across the doctrinal half: wisdom, goodness, the plan, greatness and justice, mercy, holiness, and then the one that breaks the pattern, "O that cunning plan of the evil one!" (v. 28). They function as the chapter's paragraph marks, and each one arrives after a hard fact. Jacob does not celebrate and then explain. He explains, then can't help himself.

cites.quote: O that cunning plan of the evil one!

spans.text: O that cunning plan of the evil one!

phrases.term: That awful monster, death and hell
phrases.text: Two deaths named as one creature with a grasp, and Jacob supplies the gloss himself: "which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit" (v. 10). Two verses later he separates them again so the grave delivers bodies and hell delivers spirits. The figure returns at verse 19 and verse 26 as the thing the saints are delivered from, and calling it an animal rather than a condition is what makes the rescue a rescue instead of a repair.

cites.quote: which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit

spans.text: which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit

phrases.text: Isaiah's image, where the redeemed one is covered "with the robe of righteousness" (Isa. 61:10). Jacob puts it at the far end of a sentence whose first half is worse than the source: perfect knowledge of guilt, uncleanness, and nakedness. The robe answers the nakedness exactly. Clothing at judgment is not decoration; it is the covering of the specific thing perfect knowledge exposes.

phrases.term: Endured the crosses of the world
phrases.text: The letter to the Hebrews describes Christ as having "endured the cross, despising the shame" (Heb. 12:2). Jacob applies the same two verbs to the saints and pluralizes the cross. Whether the shared wording came through the brass plates or through the prophets Jacob names, the effect here is to make discipleship the same shape as the thing endured for it.

Legal language, and the first appearance in the record of justice as a claimant with demands that must be met. The verse settles what happens to those who never received a law: the atonement pays for them, and they are "restored to that God who gave them breath" (v. 26). Later sermons in the record build whole arguments on this sentence's terms.

cites.quote: restored to that God who gave them breath

spans.text: restored to that God who gave them breath

phrases.term: O that cunning plan of the evil one!
phrases.text: The one exclamation aimed at the enemy, and it borrows the shape of the six aimed at God. Calling it a plan puts it beside "the merciful plan of the great Creator" (v. 6) as its imitation. What follows is a description of clever people talking themselves out of counsel, which suggests the plan works best on the capable.

cites.quote: the merciful plan of the great Creator

spans.text: the merciful plan of the great Creator

phrases.term: When they are learned they think they are wise
phrases.text: The chapter's most quoted sentence, and the next verse refuses the easy reading: "But to be learned is good if they hearken unto the counsels of God" (v. 29). The problem is not knowledge but the substitution of one's own supply for counsel, "supposing they know of themselves" (v. 28). Jacob, who preaches from a plate archive his family risked lives to obtain, is not against study.

cites.quote: But to be learned is good if they hearken unto the counsels of God

spans.text: But to be learned is good if they hearken unto the counsels of God

phrases.text: Paul's line to the Romans runs "to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace" (Rom. 8:6). Jacob's version trades peace for eternal life, which raises the stakes of the sentence to match his chapter. He also frames it with "remember," turning a maxim into an instruction his hearers are supposed to carry out of the meeting.

Five words with unusual consequences. Gates in the ancient world had gatekeepers, and gatekeepers can be persuaded, bribed, or fooled. Jacob removes the whole system: the Holy One of Israel keeps his own gate, "for he cannot be deceived" (v. 41). A colony whose leaders were also its priests is being told that no priest stands where it finally matters.

phrases.term: I take off my garments, and I shake them before you
phrases.text: Jacob performs the gesture in the middle of a sermon. Paul "shook his raiment" (Acts 18:6) when a synagogue rejected him, and Benjamin will tell his people he assembled them so he might "rid my garments of your blood" (Mosiah 2:28). Jacob does it before the sermon is finished, which changes its meaning: it is a witness he intends his hearers to remember at the judgment he has just described.

phrases.term: Come buy wine and milk without money and without price
phrases.text: Isaiah 55 arrives without introduction, five verses from the end. Jacob has been quoting Isaiah by announcement for three chapters; now he simply speaks in Isaiah's words, and the invitation to buy without money answers his own wo against the rich whose "treasure is their god" (v. 30). The economy of the last verses is the opposite of the one the wo-list condemned.

verses.label: v. 4–5
verses.title: An argument that begins by conceding its premises
verses.text: The record has the speaker credit the audience twice in two verses: "I know that ye know that our flesh must waste away and die," and then "I know that ye know that in the body he shall show himself unto those at Jerusalem." Nothing is being established; both points are granted before the chapter starts. What follows is inference from those two facts, which is why the doctrinal section can proceed without a single quotation of scripture until verse 50. Verse 1 also states the occasion, that the speaker has just read Isaiah aloud, so the argument is presented as commentary on a reading.

verses.label: v. 8–20
verses.title: Six exclamations, each naming a different attribute
verses.text: The record punctuates its doctrinal stretch with a recurring form: "O the wisdom of God, his mercy and grace" at verse 8, "O how great the goodness of our God" at verse 10, "O how great the plan of our God" at verse 13, "O the greatness and the justice of our God" at verse 17, "O the greatness of the mercy of our God" at verse 19, and "O how great the holiness of our God" at verse 20. Six in thirteen verses, no attribute repeated except mercy. Verse 28 then turns the same form the other way, "O that cunning plan of the evil one," so the pattern established over thirteen verses is inverted once and used against the opposite party.

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: A speaker defining his own terms as he goes
verses.text: The record has him coin and then gloss: the monster is "death and hell, which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit." Verse 11 supplies the first definition, "which death is the grave," and verse 12 the second, "which spiritual death is hell." Three definitional clauses in three verses, each introduced by a relative pronoun. The phrase "which I call" is the tell; it marks the distinction as the speaker's own construction rather than as received vocabulary, and the rest of the chapter depends on it holding.

verses.label: v. 25–27
verses.title: A chain of four conditions, then its reverse
verses.text: The record builds the argument as a linked sequence: "where there is no law given there is no punishment; and where there is no punishment there is no condemnation; and where there is no condemnation the mercies of the Holy One of Israel have claim upon them." Three links, each taking the previous conclusion as its premise, and a fourth clause supplying the ground, "because of the atonement." Verse 27 then runs the chain backward for the other case, "wo unto him that has the law given, yea, that has all the commandments of God, like unto us." The phrase "like unto us" puts the speaker and his hearers on the exposed side of his own argument.

verses.label: v. 30–38
verses.title: Nine woes with a fixed shape and varying penalties
verses.text: After the first woe at verse 27, the record delivers nine more in nine consecutive verses: the rich, the deaf, the blind, the uncircumcised of heart, the liar, the murderer, those who commit whoredoms, idolaters, and all who die in their sins. Each names a class and attaches a consequence. The consequences are not uniform: two end in perishing at verses 31 and 32, two in being thrust down to hell at verses 34 and 36, and the last supplies no punishment beyond continuance, "they shall return to God, and behold his face, and remain in their sins." The rich get the longest entry, four clauses, and the murderer the shortest.

verses.label: v. 44
verses.title: A gesture recorded inside a sermon
verses.text: The record reports a physical action, not a figure of speech: "I take off my garments, and I shake them before you." The stated purpose is evidentiary and future, "ye shall know at the last day, when all men shall be judged of their works, that the God of Israel did witness that I shook your iniquities from my soul." The same act recurs at Jacob 1:19 and 2:2 and at Mosiah 2:28, and Acts 18:6 has Paul shake his raiment with the identical logic of transferred blood-guilt. A performed act meant to be remembered as testimony is rare in these books.

chapter.title: Three movements, and the joints are visible
chapter.text: Verses 1 through 26 argue the plan, verses 27 through 38 pronounce the wos, and verses 39 through 54 plead. The exclamations mark the first movement, the repeated "wo unto" marks the second, and "O, my beloved brethren" marks the third. A hearer could feel the shape without being told it.

chapter.title: The chapter names God by one title above all others
chapter.text: "Holy One of Israel" appears thirteen times here, roughly a third of its uses in the whole record and more than any other chapter carries. The title is Isaiah's, and choosing it keeps the sermon tied to the reading it grew out of: the God who suffers, judges, and keeps the gate is the same God the prophet named.

chapter.title: It answers the question the reading left open
chapter.text: Two chapters earlier the reading asked who among them walks in darkness with no light, and stopped without the KJV's instruction to trust in the Lord's name. Jacob's whole sermon is that missing clause expanded: here is the way of deliverance, here is the gate, come buy without money. The omission looks like a plan once the sermon lands.

chapter.title: Doctrine first, then names, then invitation
chapter.text: The wo-list would be cruelty if it came first and sentiment if it came last. Placed after the plan is explained, each wo is a specific way of wasting what verses 6 through 26 just described, and placed before the plea, it gives the plea something to be merciful about.

chapter.title: The sermon argues from what the hearers already grant
chapter.text: Jacob builds on their existing knowledge four times in the opening verses, "I know that ye know" (v. 5) among them. He is not introducing the resurrection; he is drawing consequences from a belief the colony holds, and the chapter can move fast through material later writers take chapters to establish.

chapter.title: Every terror in the chapter has an exit named beside it
chapter.text: The monster has a way of escape prepared, the demands of justice are satisfied, the chains can be shaken off, the gate opens to whoever knocks. The pattern is consistent enough to be deliberate: Jacob will frighten a congregation, and he will not leave a fear on the floor without its answer.

chapter.title: The unit's center
chapter.text: Jacob's sermon runs from chapter 6 through chapter 10, and this is the chapter the others exist to frame. The reading prepared it, the next day's continuation applies it to the colony's own land and future, and the promise about seed in verse 53 is the thread that carries into chapter 10's covenant argument.

applications.title: Say the alternative out loud
applications.text: Once, in writing, finish the sentence Jacob finishes: without the resurrection and the atonement, here is where I would end. Most gratitude stays thin because the thing avoided is never specified. Specify it, then read your own exclamation.

applications.title: Audit what you are becoming
applications.text: Since judgment finds people righteous or filthy still, spend an evening on direction rather than incidents. Name one trajectory you are currently on that you would not want continued unchanged, and change one input to it this week.

applications.title: Spend the probation on something
applications.text: The wo lands on waste. Look at the last seven days and identify the hours that went nowhere on purpose. Convert one recurring slot into something that would still matter to you at the end of your life.

applications.title: Bring your learning to counsel
applications.text: Take the area where you are most competent, the one where you least expect to be corrected, and deliberately submit a decision in it to counsel this month, from scripture, a leader, or someone qualified to disagree with you. Verse 29 keeps the competence; verse 28 warns about where it gets used.

applications.title: Check the treasure sentence
applications.text: Jacob's test for wealth is the direction of the heart: whose treasure is whose god. List where your money went last month and see what the list would tell a stranger about your loyalties.

applications.title: Knock without credentials
applications.text: Try one prayer this week in which you present nothing, no record of service, no explanation of your usefulness. The gate in this chapter opens to knocking, and the things people usually bring to it are the things verse 42 asks them to put down.

applications.title: Shake one thing loose
applications.text: Jacob's gesture was public and physical. Pick a chain you have been carrying and do something bodily about it: a conversation, a deletion, a returned item, a confession. The verse pairs turning away from sin with shaking off, and the second half is an action.

questions.text: What have I actually settled about my own death, and what am I still avoiding thinking through?
Which of the two deaths frightens me more, and what does my answer say about what I believe is at stake?
If nothing about my direction changed, what would "still" mean in my case?
What am I spending the days of my probation on that I could not defend at the judgment Jacob just described?
Where do I suppose I know of myself, and whose counsel have I stopped asking for?
What would I have to cast away to come down into the depths of humility, and why does the list feel so expensive?
What am I still paying for that this chapter says is free?
